extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, empirical researchers, patent policy analysts, and USPTO policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: An empirical analysis of how USPTO examiner time allocations (proxied by GS-level and technology group) affect the incidence of federal litigation and PTAB proceedings for patent applications, and a cost–benefit style calculation of litigation/PTAB savings from doubling examiner time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conditional negative binomial regression for count outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the rarity and count-like structure of the litigation outcomes (i.e., measures that take on integer levels greater than or equal to zero), we do not estimate Ordinary Least Squares regressions but instead estimate conditional negative binomial regression models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate for dependent variables that are nonnegative integer counts with overdispersion. Do not use OLS for such outcomes. Report coefficients as incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and interpret multiplicatively (e.g., IRR 1.26 ⇒ 26% higher rate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regress litigation/PTAB counts on GS-level dummy variables
rubrics_metrics.description: We capture the relationship by regressing the number of times the application is asserted in litigation on dummy variables for the different GS-levels—e.g., a dichotomous variable indicating whether the associated examiner is at GS-level 7, ... GS-level 9, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use GS-level dummies (with a reference category, here GS-7) rather than an assumed linear hours effect to flexibly map GS-level → time allocation → outcome. Compare specific GS-levels (e.g., GS-14 vs GS-7) to simulate halving/doubling time allocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include technology-group fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Within this regression framework, we include fixed effects for the technology group to which the examiner is assigned, such that we account for fixed differences in litigation frequencies across technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This forces comparisons of GS-levels to be made within technology groups, avoiding confounding from cross-technology differences in litigation propensity. Do not attempt to identify hour effects solely from across-technology variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for temporal and examiner characteristics via fixed effects
rubrics_metrics.description: We also include a series of fixed effects for the following factors: (1) the year in which the application is disposed of; (2) the experience level of the examiner (in two-year bins); (3) the year in which the examiner joined the Patent Office; and (4) the ultimate tenure of the examiner at the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These controls help isolate the time-allocation aspect of GS-level promotions and account for cohort, experience, training, and tenure effects that could confound GS-level → litigation relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus baseline analysis on filed applications (not just issued patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since our goal is to understand how doubling time allocations for all examiners may lead to a reduction in overall litigation, we attempt to capture both mechanisms by estimating the relationship in question using a sample of filed applications (as distinct from issued patents) as the baseline sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using applications captures effects via (1) fewer patents issued overall and (2) fewer invalid patents issued. Still report robustness estimates limited to issued patents to probe mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample restriction to allow observing litigation outcomes (exclude recent dispositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: We focus our estimation sample on those patent applications that were disposed of prior to 2014. We exclude dispositions subsequent to this point as there is generally a notable gap in time between when patents issue and when we observe assertions in federal court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids attenuating results by including applications without sufficient follow-up to observe litigation. Report robustness including all applications to show sensitivity (authors report virtually identical results when including all 3.9M applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret coefficients as incidence rate ratios (IRR)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reported coefficients are to be interpreted as incidence rate ratios (“IRR”). For instance, the estimated IRR of 1.26 for the GS-level 9 coefficient suggests that the applications reviewed by GS-level 9 examiners are litigated at 1.26 times the rate of applications reviewed by the reference group—i.e., GS-level 7 examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present IRRs with standard errors; translate IRR differences into percentage increases/decreases for substantive interpretation (IRR 1.78 ⇒ +78%; inverse interpretations for doubling/halving exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use GS-level comparisons to simulate halving/doubling of time allocations
rubrics_metrics.description: Given that examination time falls by almost exactly half as examiners ascend from GS-level 7 to GS-level 14, comparing the litigation outcomes between these two levels provides us with an opportunity to explore the effect of cutting—or doubling, when considering the relationship in reverse—the assigned examination time in half.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directly observe coefficient for GS-14 (relative to GS-7) to simulate cut-in-half; reverse comparison simulates doubling time. Note this leverages observed GS → hours mapping across technology groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness: limit sample to issued patents to probe mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: In unreported regressions, we also estimate specifications where we limit the sample to issued patents. In this alternative approach, we estimate a similar pattern of increasing rates of litigation as examiners ascend GS-levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If results persist when limiting to issued patents, part of the effect likely operates through marginally issued invalid patents being more likely to be litigated. Always report robustness and mechanism checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative hours variable (parametric hours approach) as robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: We assign a variable to each application equal to the number of hours allotted to the associated examiner based on the GS-level and technology group of that examiner, then estimate the negative binomial model replacing GS-level dummies with this sample-hours variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is less flexible and more parametric (assumes linear hours relationship). It may misrepresent doubling for technology groups with above/below-average hours; leave as a robustness exercise rather than preferred specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drop rare GS-level categories if necessary (e.g., GS-5 and GS-15)
rubrics_metrics.description: We drop GS-level 5 and GS-level 15 examiners from our analysis, though we note that this decision has little to no bearing on our results and the conclusions we reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit extremely rare categories that could destabilize estimation; report that dropping them does not change substantive conclusions and point to Online Appendix for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cluster standard errors to correct for within-examiner autocorrelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard errors are reported in parentheses and are clustered to correct for autocorrelation within given examiners over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cluster at the examiner level (or other appropriate panel unit) when observations are correlated over time for the same examiner to obtain valid inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report statistical significance notation and sample N
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimates marked with *, **, and *** are significant at 10%, 5%, and 1%, respectively. Each observation is a given application from the PAIR database that reached a final disposition and that was published in the PAIR records between March 2001 and December 2014.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always report sample size (N), data window, significance markers, and what database(s) were used (PAIR, Lex Machina, PTAB data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple data sources for litigation cost estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: For litigation-cost savings we draw on: (1) AIPLA economic survey (costs by stage and amounts at stake); (2) Cotropia et al.'s granular analysis of civil litigation (distribution of terminations across stages); and (3) Lex Machina data on patent infringement lawsuits (including damages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple complementary datasets to construct a probability distribution over lawsuit types (stakes × termination stage) and associated costs; be explicit about which costs are included (authors used defense-side AIPLA costs and assumed plaintiff costs match defense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute cost per patent-lawsuit pair by dividing average lawsuit cost by average patents per case
rubrics_metrics.description: We estimate the total litigation costs associated with an average lawsuit is $539,949. To determine the average cost per patent-lawsuit pair, we divide this estimate by the average number of patents that are included in each case filing over our sample period (2.3 years) to arrive at an estimated cost per patent-lawsuit pair ($234,761).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When lawsuits involve multiple patents, allocate average lawsuit cost across patents (or otherwise justify allocation). Report assumptions (here average patents per case = 2.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate estimated incidence reductions into monetary savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiply the predicted reduction in number of patent-lawsuit pairs (e.g., 2,436 fewer pairs per year from doubling hours) by the estimated cost per patent-lawsuit pair to obtain annual litigation savings (here ≈ $572 million).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the baseline number of annual dispositions (here 430,056) and predicted reduction (from IRR comparisons) to compute forgone pairs, then monetize using cost-per-pair estimate. Present intermediate table (number of reviews, expected pairs, reduction, dollar savings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discount future litigation savings using OMB recommended rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculating the present value of future litigation savings requires: (1) how far into the future the litigation savings will materialize and (2) the appropriate discount rate. We elect to utilize the discount rates suggested by the Office of Management and Budget of 3% and 7%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate timing of cost realization (authors estimate expenses occur roughly 5.2 years following issuance) and compute present values at multiple discount rates (3% and 7%) to show sensitivity (example: $572M presently valued at $491M at 3% and $402M at 7%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate timing of litigation expenses from issuance to expense realization
rubrics_metrics.description: We find that on average patents experience their first litigation filing 3.1 years following the date of allowance; considering distribution of repeat litigations and time to discovery milestones (22 months on average), expenses occur roughly 5.2 years following the date of patent issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical distributions of time-to-litigation and stage durations (e.g., Cotropia et al.) to time when costs are incurred for discounting. Be explicit about which milestones (filing, discovery, claim construction) drive expense timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess PTAB as potential substitute and include PTAB outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent that PTAB creates a substitute for the litigation of a patent's validity in federal courts, one may be concerned that PTAB would dampen the relationship between examination time and the degree of litigation savings. We thus examine whether PTAB is a substitute and estimate the effect of GS-level changes on PTAB institutions (outcome: number of times application was the subject of a PTAB challenge up to March 2016).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare pre-/post-AIA litigation rates, examine overlap between PTAB institutions and federal litigation, and estimate analogous negative binomial models with PTAB institution counts as the dependent variable. Note PTAB baseline rates are lower (noisier estimates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify overlap effects and conservatively adjust savings if necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Because some forgone patent-lawsuit pairs may overlap contemporaneously with PTAB challenges (leading to stayed litigation and lower costs), consider the fraction of overlapping cases and the potential downward adjustment to savings (authors estimate overlap ≤7% and a conservative $31M reduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly calculate overlap fraction (PTAB institution rate / litigation rate) and model conservative adjustments (e.g., assume overlapping litigation costs are half) to assess sensitivity of savings estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prior research to justify omitting examiner fixed effects when computationally burdensome
rubrics_metrics.description: In Table 2, we do not include examiner fixed effects because including examiner effects and technology-group fixed effects in a conditional negative binomial regression with over three million observations represents a rather cumbersome estimation exercise. Nonetheless, in our prior research on grant rates we found that accounting for disposition year effects, examiner hiring year effects, examiner tenure effects, and examiner experience effects leads to estimates that are virtually identical to estimates that include examiner fixed effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computational limits preclude including fine-grained fixed effects (e.g., individual examiner FE), include proxies/cohort and tenure fixed effects and cite robustness from prior studies showing similar results. Report this limitation and supporting evidence.
